tools.title: BloodHound (AD Attack Paths)
usage: bloodhound-python -d domain.local -u user -p pass -c all -dc dc01.domain.local
tools.description: Uses graph theory to reveal hidden attack paths in Active Directory/Azure environments.
tools.notes: Collection queries LDAP/SMB with credentials you were issued and generates JSON you import into the BloodHound UI to map attack paths. Only run against a domain you are explicitly authorized to assess or your own lab domain.

tools.title: NetExec — nxc (Network Pentesting)
tools.description: Swiss army knife for pentesting Windows/AD networks. Successor to CrackMapExec.
tools.notes: nxc authenticates and enumerates Windows/AD hosts; spraying and hash-dumping are credential attacks. Sweeping a whole subnet touches every host in it — confirm the full range is in scope. Authorized engagements or your own lab only.

tools.title: Impacket (Network Protocol Tools)
usage: AS-REP roast users with no pre-auth
tools.description: Python classes for working with SMB, MSRPC, Kerberos, LDAP, and more.
tools.notes: Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, secretsdump and the *exec modules are active credential-theft and remote-execution attacks against a domain. Run only where you have written authorization or in your own lab domain.

tools.title: Responder (LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoner)
tools.description: LLMNR/NBT-NS/MDNS poisoner with rogue authentication servers for credential capture.
tools.notes: Responder answers broadcast name-resolution requests to capture NetNTLM hashes (logged under /usr/share/responder/logs). It actively poisons the local segment and affects every host on it — only run on a network you are authorized to attack. Use -A analyze mode first to observe without poisoning.

tools.title: Certipy (AD Certificate Abuse)
usage: request a certificate from a template
certipy req -u user@domain.local -p pass -ca CA-NAME -template TemplateName -dc-ip 10.10.10.10
authenticate with a PFX (get TGT / NT hash)
tools.description: Active Directory Certificate Services enumeration and abuse tool.
tools.notes: Certipy enumerates and abuses AD Certificate Services (ESC1-ESC8) to escalate privileges or forge authentication. Requesting/abusing certificates is an active attack — authorized engagements or your own lab CA only.

tools.title: Kerbrute (Kerberos Brute Force)
tools.description: Kerberos pre-auth brute-forcer for username enumeration and password spraying.
tools.notes: Kerbrute uses Kerberos pre-auth, so username enumeration is quiet, but spraying and brute-force can lock out domain accounts — mind the lockout policy. Authorized engagements or your own lab domain only.

tools.title: ldapdomaindump (AD LDAP Dumper)
tools.description: Dumps AD users, groups, computers, policies and trusts over LDAP into browsable HTML/JSON/greppable output — great for offline domain enumeration.
tools.notes: Authenticated LDAP reads are low-impact enumeration, but they still use domain credentials against a live DC — run only against a domain you are authorized to assess or your own lab. Point -o at an empty directory.

tools.title: Coercer (Authentication Coercion)
tools.description: Automatically coerces a Windows host to authenticate to an attacker-controlled listener across many RPC methods (MS-RPRN / PetitPotam / DFSCoerce / …), feeding NTLM relay or hash capture.
tools.notes: Coercion forces a target to authenticate to you — pair it with Responder / ntlmrelayx to capture or relay those credentials. It actively triggers auth on a live host, so authorized targets only. Run `scan` first to see what's exploitable before `coerce`.

tools.title: PCredz (Credential Extractor)
tools.description: Harvests credentials from live traffic or pcap files — NTLM (HTTP/SMB/LDAP/SQL), Kerberos AS-REQ, and even credit-card numbers. Great for mining Responder / relay captures.
tools.notes: Parsing your own pcap files is passive and safe. Live capture needs root and only sees traffic on a network you're authorized to monitor. Depends on pcapy-ng (`pip3 install pcapy-ng`, plus libpcap-dev). Feeds nicely off Responder captures.

tools.title: The Hacker Recipes (AD)
tools.description: Maintained, well-organized methodology for Active Directory attacks — recon, movement, credential theft, Kerberos and ADCS — with the exact tool commands for each step.

tools.title: Anonymously Surf
usage: get a fresh Tor circuit / new IP
tools.description:
It automatically overwrites the RAM when the system shuts down
and also changes your IP address.
tools.notes: anonsurf transparently forces the whole host through Tor, so every process is affected, not just your browser — verify with `anonsurf myip` before trusting it. Needs root (iptables). Tor exit traffic is slow and some services block Tor; only tunnel activity you are authorized to route.

tools.title: Multitor
usage: spawn N Tor instances behind a load balancer
tools.description: How to stay in multi places at the same time.
tools.notes: multitor runs several Tor processes and rotates between them behind HAProxy/Privoxy, giving many exit IPs at once — useful for spreading authorized scanning/OSINT so no single circuit is hammered. Runs as the dedicated tor user (`--user debian-tor`); still slow, and rotating IPs does not make out-of-scope targets in-scope.

tools.title: Tor + torsocks (SOCKS anonymity proxy)
usage: run any single command through Tor
confirm the exit IP is a Tor node
tunnel an SSH session over Tor
tools.description: The Tor daemon plus torsocks, which transparently pushes any single command through Tor's SOCKS proxy (default 127.0.0.1:9050).
tools.notes: torsocks wraps only the command you prefix — unwrapped tools still leak your real IP, so confirm with the check.torproject.org line. UDP and ICMP cannot go through Tor (no `torsocks nmap -sU`, no ping). Keep it to authorized recon; Tor is slow and many targets rate-limit or block exits.

tools.title: proxychains-ng (chain traffic through proxies/Tor)
usage: route a command through the configured chain
proxy an Nmap connect scan (TCP only)
tools.description: Forces a program's TCP connections through a chain of SOCKS/HTTP proxies (or Tor) defined in proxychains4.conf.
tools.notes: proxychains hijacks TCP only via LD_PRELOAD; Nmap must use `-sT -Pn` (SYN/UDP/ping bypass the proxy and leak your IP). Edit /etc/proxychains4.conf to point at Tor's 9050 socks and set `proxy_dns` to avoid DNS leaks. Chain only through proxies you are authorized to use, against authorized targets.

tools.title: Whonix — Anonymity & Tor OpSec (docs)
tools.description: Practical, tool-agnostic guidance on staying anonymous with Tor: leak vectors, DNS/UDP pitfalls, and what Tor does and does not protect.

tools.title: Prowler (Cloud Security Scanner)
tools.description: Open-source security tool for AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes assessments.
tools.notes: Only assess accounts/subscriptions you own or are explicitly authorized to test. Prowler is read-only, but it calls hundreds of cloud APIs — that generates CloudTrail/audit-log entries and can incur API-call costs. Start with a scoped profile/region rather than a whole org.

tools.title: ScoutSuite (Multi-Cloud Auditing)
usage: audit AWS with a named profile
tools.description: Multi-cloud security auditing tool for AWS, Azure, GCP, Alibaba, and Oracle.
tools.notes: Authorized accounts only. ScoutSuite enumerates your cloud config via read-only API calls and writes a static HTML report to ./scoutsuite-report/ — no changes to the environment, but the API calls are logged. Review the report locally.

tools.title: Pacu (AWS Exploitation Framework)
tools.description: AWS exploitation framework for offensive security testing of AWS environments.
tools.notes: Pacu is an OFFENSIVE AWS framework — its modules actively enumerate, exploit misconfigurations, escalate privilege and can modify resources. Run it only against AWS accounts you own or have written authorization to attack. Work inside its interactive shell (`list`/`search`/`run <module>`); some modules are noisy and leave audit-log evidence.

tools.title: Trivy (Container/K8s Scanner)
tools.description: Comprehensive vulnerability scanner for containers, Kubernetes, IaC, and code.
tools.notes: Image/filesystem/config scans are fully local and read-only — safe to run anywhere. Trivy downloads its vulnerability DB on first run (needs network). Scan only images and repos you're authorized to assess.

tools.title: Checkov (IaC Misconfig Scanner)
tools.description: Static analysis for infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, ARM, Dockerfiles) that flags insecure cloud configuration before deploy.
tools.notes: Checkov reads your IaC files statically and never touches a live cloud account or makes API calls — completely safe and offline. Ideal in CI to catch insecure defaults (public buckets, open security groups) before they ship.

tools.title: HackTricks Cloud (cloud pentest playbook)
tools.description: The cloud-focused HackTricks book — AWS/GCP/Azure/Kubernetes enumeration, privilege-escalation and post-exploitation techniques with copy-paste commands.

tools.title: flaws.cloud (AWS Security Challenge)
tools.description: A free hands-on AWS security lab that walks through common S3/IAM misconfigurations as a CTF — a safe, authorized target to practice cloud recon on.

tools.title: DDoS
usage: run the script from its clone dir
tools.description: Best DDoS Attack Script With 36 Plus Methods. DDoS attacks for SECURITY TESTING PURPOSES ONLY!
tools.notes: A multi-method flood script — legal ONLY against a target you own or are explicitly authorized to test in an isolated lab. Flooding any system you don't control is a crime. It takes a thread count and a timer: start with a low thread count and a short duration, watch the target, then stop.

tools.title: SlowLoris
usage: hold connections open against a host
tools.description: Slowloris is basically an HTTP Denial of Service attack. It sends lots of HTTP requests.
tools.notes: Slowloris is a low-bandwidth Layer-7 attack: it ties up a web server's worker pool by opening many partial HTTP requests and never finishing them. Run it ONLY against your own lab server. Control the load with -s (sockets) and stop with Ctrl-C — a small -s already exhausts an unhardened server.

tools.title: Asyncrone | Multifunction SYN Flood DDoS Weapon
tools.description:
aSYNcrone is a C language based, multifunction SYN Flood DDoS Weapon.
Disable the destination system by sending SYN packets intensively.

tools.title: UFOnet
tools.description: UFONet is a free software, P2P and cryptographic disruptive toolkit that allows performing DoS and DDoS attacks.
tools.notes: UFONet drives a botnet of "zombie" open-redirect/proxy hosts to amplify a DDoS. Only ever aim it at infrastructure you own or are authorized to test. Recruiting or abusing third-party zombie hosts is illegal even if the final target is yours. Kept to the GUI/help launch — exact attack flags vary by version, so read `ufonet --help` in your installed build before firing.

tools.title: GoldenEye
usage: run an HTTP DoS test against a URL
tools.description:
GoldenEye is a python3 app for SECURITY TESTING PURPOSES ONLY!
GoldenEye is a HTTP DoS Test Tool.
Usage: ./goldeneye.py <url> [OPTIONS]

tools.title: SaphyraDDoS
tools.description: A Python DDoS script for SECURITY TESTING PURPOSES ONLY.
tools.notes: A single-file Python HTTP flooder. Authorized targets / your own lab ONLY. It takes just a URL and floods until you Ctrl-C, so there is no built-in rate limit — run it on an isolated network and stop it manually.

tools.title: hping3 (Packet Crafter / Flooder)
usage: send 5 SYN packets to a port
tools.description: Command-line TCP/IP packet crafter and analyzer — sends custom SYN/UDP/ICMP packets, the classic tool for controlled SYN-flood and firewall/latency testing.
tools.notes: Raw sockets need root, so this asks for sudo — the minimum needed to craft packets. --flood sends as fast as possible with NO reply wait: only use it against your own lab host. Prefer -c (packet count) or -i (interval) to keep the rate controlled while you measure the target's response.

tools.title: slowhttptest (Slow-HTTP DoS Tester)
usage: bound the run and save a report
tools.description: Configurable Layer-7 slow-HTTP attack simulator (slowloris, slow POST body, slow read, range) for testing how well a web server survives low-bandwidth DoS.
tools.notes: The safe, measurable counterpart to slowloris — it prints a live availability graph so you can see exactly when your own server stops responding. Authorized/own-lab targets ONLY. Bound every run with -l (seconds) and keep -c (connections) modest; -g -o writes an HTML/CSV report.

tools.title: OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet
tools.description: OWASP's guidance on how DoS/DDoS attacks work and the application- and network-layer defenses to test for — the blue-team companion to these tools.

tools.title: RouterSploit
tools.description: The RouterSploit Framework is an open-source exploitation framework dedicated to embedded devices
tools.notes: RouterSploit targets embedded/IoT devices (routers, cameras) — exploits can crash or brick real hardware, so run only against authorized lab devices you can reset. The console verbs (use/set/run/search) mirror Metasploit.

 Usage: python commix.py [option(s)]
tools.notes: Commix confirms and exploits OS command injection — --os-shell runs real commands on the target host, so use it only where you're authorized. Start without --os-shell to just confirm the vuln, then escalate.

tools.description:
The world's most widely used memory forensics framework.
Usage: python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.pslist
tools.notes: Volatility reads a memory image offline and never touches a live system — safe on any dump you're authorized to examine. Plugins are namespaced by OS (windows.* / linux.* / mac.*); run `vol.py -f dump windows.info` first to confirm the profile.

tools.title: Binwalk (Firmware Analysis)
tools.description:
Analyze, reverse engineer, and extract firmware images.
Usage: binwalk -e firmware.bin
tools.notes: Scanning and extracting are read-only on the input image. -Me can unpack deeply nested archives and fill the disk, so extract into a scratch directory. Great for pulling filesystems and configs out of router/IoT firmware.

tools.title: pspy (Process Monitor — No Root)
tools.description: Monitor Linux processes without root — detects cron jobs, scheduled tasks, other users' commands.
tools.notes: pspy is passive — it snapshots /proc to reveal cron jobs and commands run by other users without needing root, and changes nothing on the host. Ideal on a box you already have a foothold on to catch privileged scheduled tasks.

tools.title: ExifTool (Metadata)
tools.description: The standard tool for reading, writing and stripping metadata (EXIF/IPTC/XMP/GPS) across images, PDFs, office docs and video.
tools.notes: Reading metadata is passive and safe. Writing/stripping (-all=, -TAG=) edits the file in place (it keeps a *_original backup) — copy evidence first. GPS/timestamp fields are gold for OSINT and CTF stego challenges.

tools.title: Foremost (File Carving)
tools.description: Recovers files from disk images or raw data by carving on file headers/footers — recovers deleted files with no filesystem.
tools.notes: Foremost only reads the input image and writes recovered files to -o (which must not already exist) — non-destructive on the evidence. Handy for recovering deleted files in disk-forensics and CTF challenges.

tools.title: reconFTW (Automated Recon)

recon a list of domains to a dir

tools.title: EyeWitness (Web Screenshots + Headers)

write the report to a folder

tools.notes: Frida instruments a live process, so it needs a rooted/jailbroken test device or emulator with a matching frida-server running (-U talks to it over USB). Only hook apps you own or are explicitly authorized to test.

tools.title: Objection (Mobile Runtime Exploration)
usage: explore with SSL pinning disabled at start
patch an APK with the Frida gadget (no root)
tools.description: Runtime mobile exploration toolkit powered by Frida — no jailbreak/root required.
tools.notes: Objection is powered by Frida — the `explore` flow needs frida-server on a rooted/jailbroken device or emulator; `patchapk` embeds the gadget so a non-rooted device works instead. Runtime changes (pinning/root bypass) are per-session and non-persistent. Authorized apps only.

tools.title: adb (Android Debug Bridge)
usage: pull an installed app's APK off the device
tools.description: Android Debug Bridge — the core CLI for talking to Android devices/emulators: install/pull APKs, shell, and read logs.
tools.notes: adb needs USB debugging enabled on the device; use it only on test devices/emulators and apps you own or are authorized to assess. `adb shell` runs as the shell user (not root) unless the device is rooted — no blanket privilege is required for install/pull/logcat.

tools.title: OWASP MAS (Mobile App Security)

tools.title: Frida CodeShare

tools.title: HatCloud(Bypass CloudFlare for IP)

tools.title: zsteg (PNG/BMP LSB detector)
tools.description: Detects LSB stego, hidden text and appended data in PNG/BMP images — the first thing to run on a suspicious PNG.
tools.notes: Ruby gem, offline. Only handles PNG and BMP (use steghide/stegseek for JPEG/WAV). `-a` tries all channel/bit-order combos and is the usual first pass; `-E` extracts once you know the channel string zsteg reported.

tools.title: outguess (JPEG stego)
usage: hide a file in a JPEG
tools.description: Classic redundancy-preserving steganography for JPEG; a common alternative to steghide in CTF challenges.
tools.notes: Offline file operation. If steghide/zsteg find nothing on a JPEG, try outguess — challenges often pick one specific tool, so cycle through them.

tools.title: ExifTool (metadata reader)
tools.description: Reads/writes metadata in images, PDFs and media; flags live in EXIF comments, GPS and maker-note fields more often than you'd think.
tools.notes: Read-only by default and fully offline. Always the cheapest first check on any media file — look at Comment, Artist, Software and GPS fields before pulling out the heavy stego tooling.

tools.title: Aperi'Solve (all-in-one image stego)
tools.description: Upload an image and it runs zsteg, steghide, binwalk, exiftool, foremost and layer/bit-plane analysis in one pass — the fastest triage for a mystery image.

tools.title: StegOnline (in-browser LSB explorer)
tools.description: Browser tool to toggle bit planes / colour channels, extract LSB data and view image layers — no upload to a server needed.

tools.title: Futureboy Stegano decoder
tools.description: Classic online steghide-style hide/reveal service; handy when you can't install steghide locally.

tools.title: stego-toolkit (Docker kit + checklist)
tools.description: DominicBreuker's Docker image bundling ~all common stego/forensics tools plus a practical 'which tool for which file' checklist — the reference to keep open during a CTF.

tools.title: Web2Attack
tools.description: Web hacking framework with tools, exploits by python

Skipfish – Fully automated, active web application security reconnaissance tool

tools.title: SubDomain Finder
tools.description:
Sublist3r is a python tool designed to enumerate subdomains of websites using OSINT 
 Usage:
	[1] python3 sublist3r.py -d example.com 
[2] python3 sublist3r.py -d example.com -p 80,443
tools.notes: The default run is passive — it only queries public OSINT/search sources, so it's safe pre-engagement recon. -b adds active DNS queries; still light. Only enumerate domains you're authorized to test.

tools.title: CheckURL

Detect evil urls that uses IDN Homograph Attack.
	[!] python3 checkURL.py --url google.com

tools.title: Blazy(Also Find ClickJacking)

tools.title: Sub-Domain TakeOver

Sub-domain takeover vulnerability occur when a sub-domain 
 (subdomain.example.com) is pointing to a service (e.g: GitHub, AWS/S3,..)
that has been removed or deleted.

tools.notes: Only inspects CNAME chains and service fingerprints of dangling records — very low traffic and non-destructive. Confirm a flagged takeover manually before reporting, and stay within authorized domains.

tools.title: Dirb
tools.description:
DIRB is a Web Content Scanner. It looks for existing (and/or hidden) Web Objects.
It basically works by launching a dictionary based attack against 
 a web server and analyzing the response.
tools.notes: Directory brute-forcing sends one request per word — use -z to add a delay so you don't flood a small lab box. Scope to the single target URL; -c passes a session cookie for authenticated areas.

tools.title: Nuclei (Vulnerability Scanner)
tools.description:
Fast, template-based vulnerability scanner used by 50k+ security teams.
Usage: nuclei -u https://example.com
tools.notes: Run `nuclei -update-templates` first. Some templates are intrusive — narrow with -severity/-tags and throttle with -rl and -c on lab networks. Templates only hit the hosts you pass; scope to authorized targets.

tools.title: ffuf (Web Fuzzer)
tools.description:
Fast web fuzzer — content discovery, parameter fuzzing, vhost discovery.
Usage: ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u https://example.com/FUZZ
tools.notes: Use -rate (and -p for a per-request delay) so you don't hammer a lab VM, and -fc/-fs/-mc to filter noise. FUZZ marks the injection point; scope the URL to the authorized target.

tools.title: Feroxbuster (Directory Brute Force)
tools.description:
Fast, recursive content discovery tool written in Rust.
Usage: feroxbuster -u https://example.com -w wordlist.txt
tools.notes: Recursion is on by default and can explode request counts — cap it with -d and throttle with --rate-limit on small boxes. Scope -u to the single authorized host.

tools.title: Nikto (Web Server Scanner)
tools.description:
Scan web servers for dangerous files, outdated software, misconfigurations.
Usage: nikto -h https://example.com
tools.notes: Nikto is deliberately noisy (thousands of probes) and will trip IDS — expected and fine in a lab. Scope -h to the target; use -Pause to slow down and -Tuning to run only the checks you need.

tools.title: wafw00f (WAF Detector)
tools.description:
Fingerprint and identify Web Application Firewalls (WAF).
Usage: wafw00f https://example.com
tools.notes: Sends only a handful of probe requests, so it's a light, safe first step before heavier scanning. Knowing the WAF up front tells you what evasion/throttling you may need.

tools.title: Katana (Web Crawler)
tools.description:
Next-generation crawling and spidering framework from ProjectDiscovery.
Usage: katana -u https://example.com
tools.notes: Request volume scales with site size — cap with -d and throttle with -rl/-rate on labs. Crawling only touches the target you pass; feed its output into ffuf or nuclei. Scope to authorized hosts.

tools.title: Gobuster (Dir/DNS/Vhost Brute Force)
tools.description: Directory/file, DNS, and vhost brute-forcing tool written in Go.
tools.notes: Throttle with --delay and lower -t (threads) on small VMs. dns mode queries resolvers rather than the host itself; dir/vhost hit the target directly, so scope -u to the authorized host.

tools.title: Dirsearch (Web Path Discovery)
tools.description: Web path brute-forcing tool for discovering directories and files on web servers.
tools.notes: Keep -t low and add --delay to be gentle on lab boxes; avoid -r (recursive) on large sites to limit request volume. Scope -u to the single authorized target.

tools.title: OWASP ZAP (Web App Scanner)
usage: scripted quick scan to a report
tools.description: Full-featured web application security scanner — proxy, spider, fuzzer, scanner.
tools.notes: Passive spidering/scanning is gentle and safe. The ACTIVE scan sends real attack payloads — run it only against authorized targets and set the ZAP context/scope so it can't wander off the box.

tools.title: testssl.sh (TLS/SSL Checker)
tools.description: Check TLS/SSL ciphers, protocols, and cryptographic flaws on any port.
tools.notes: Only negotiates TLS handshakes — no exploitation and very light traffic, so it's safe against any authorized host. Great for spotting weak ciphers/protocols (Heartbleed, POODLE, etc.) without touching the app.

tools.title: Arjun (HTTP Parameter Discovery)
tools.description: HTTP parameter discovery suite that finds hidden GET/POST parameters.
tools.notes: Arjun guesses params in bulk, so it fires many requests — add -T (per-request timeout) and keep threads modest on lab boxes. Point it at one authorized endpoint at a time.

tools.title: Caido (Web Security Auditing)
tools.description: Lightweight, modern web security auditing toolkit — Burp Suite alternative written in Rust.

tools.title: mitmproxy (Intercepting Proxy)
tools.description: Interactive TLS-capable intercepting HTTP proxy for pentesters and developers.
tools.notes: mitmproxy only sees traffic you route through it — set your browser/system proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080 and install its CA cert for TLS. Only intercept traffic to authorized targets; it forwards nothing until you let it.

tools.title: WhatWeb (Web Fingerprinter)
tools.description: Identifies web technologies — CMS, frameworks, servers, JS libs — via 1800+ plugins.
tools.notes: -a 1 (passive/stealthy) sends a single request; -a 3/-a 4 add extra probes but traffic stays light. Knowing the stack up front points you at the right exploit path. Scope to authorized targets.

tools.title: WPScan (WordPress Scanner)
usage: use the vuln DB (free API token)
tools.description: Black-box WordPress security scanner — enumerates users, plugins, themes and known CVEs.
tools.notes: Enumeration is active (many requests) — use --throttle and scope --url to the target. The -P password attack hammers the login form, so run it only against authorized boxes. A free WPScan API token unlocks real CVE data.

tools.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy
tools.description: Free, hands-on labs + guides for every major web vuln class, from the makers of Burp Suite.

tools.title: PayloadsAllTheThings
tools.description: Massive repo of payloads and bypass techniques for web attacks — SQLi, XSS, SSTI, SSRF, upload, and more.

tools.title: HackTricks
tools.description: Go-to pentest wiki: methodology and copy-paste commands for web, network, cloud and privilege escalation.

tools.title: revshells.com (Reverse Shell Generator)
tools.description: Generate reverse/bind shell one-liners in any language with your IP/port — plus listener and upgrade tips.

tools.title: WiFi-Pumpkin
tools.description:
The WiFi-Pumpkin is a rogue AP framework to easily create fake networks
while forwarding legitimate traffic to and from the unsuspecting target.
tools.notes: Stands up a rogue AP that intercepts traffic — only run it on a network and for clients you own or are explicitly authorized to test. Broadcasting a fake SSID near third parties is illegal. Use an isolated lab SSID and your own client device.

tools.title: pixiewps
usage: put your adapter in monitor mode
tools.description:
Pixiewps is a tool written in C used to bruteforce offline the WPS pin
exploiting the low or non-existing entropy of some Access Points (pixie dust attack).
tools.notes: The pixie-dust computation is offline, but capturing the WPS exchange (reaver) transmits to a live AP — only target your own router. Many modern APs lock WPS after failed attempts; test on a lab AP with WPS deliberately enabled.

tools.title: Bluetooth Honeypot GUI Framework
usage: confirm your BT adapter is up
run the honeypot (needs a BT receiver)
tools.description:
You need at least 1 bluetooth receiver.
Install libbluetooth-dev (Ubuntu) / bluez-libs-devel (Fedora) / bluez-devel (openSUSE).
tools.notes: A defensive/research honeypot — it listens for Bluetooth connections. Run it on hardware you own; only log devices you are authorized to observe. Requires a working Bluetooth receiver and a JRE.

tools.title: Fluxion
usage: # menu: pick interface -> scan all channels
tools.description: Fluxion is a remake of linset by vk496 with enhanced functionality.
tools.notes: Evil-twin + captive portal that tricks a user into typing the WiFi password — strictly your own network and your own test client. Deauthing or phishing users of a network you don't own is illegal. Keep it in an isolated lab.

tools.title: Wifiphisher
usage: auto-run and pick a target AP
set the AP and jamming interfaces
tools.description:
Wifiphisher is a rogue Access Point framework for conducting red team engagements
or Wi-Fi security testing. Easily achieve man-in-the-middle position against
wireless clients by performing targeted Wi-Fi association attacks.
tools.notes: Performs targeted association attacks and serves fake portals — authorized red team engagements or your own lab only. Two adapters (one AP, one deauth) are typical. Never target real users or nearby networks.

tools.title: Wifite
usage: skip WPS and crack with a wordlist
tools.description: Wifite is an automated wireless attack tool.
tools.notes: Automates airmon/airodump/aireplay/aircrack and will deauth clients by default — only run against an AP you own. Prefer --pmkid to avoid deauthing, and scope to a single --bssid so you never touch neighbouring networks.

tools.title: EvilTwin

tools.title: Fastssh

Fastssh — multi-threaded scan and brute force attack against SSH protocol
using the most commonly used credentials.

tools.title: Howmanypeople

Count the number of people around you by monitoring wifi signals.
[@] WIFI ADAPTER REQUIRED

tools.notes: Passively counts nearby devices from WiFi probe traffic. Monitoring MAC addresses on networks you don't own may be illegal in your jurisdiction — use only where you are authorized. Needs an adapter that supports monitor mode.

tools.title: Airgeddon (Wireless Attack Suite)
usage: # menu: select interface -> Put in monitor mode
tools.description:
Multi-use bash script for auditing wireless networks.
Covers WPA/WPA2, WEP, WPS, PMKID, evil twin, handshake capture and more.
tools.notes: A menu wrapper around aircrack-ng/hcxdumptool/hashcat — the same authorized-only rules apply. Its deauth and evil-twin modes hit live clients; keep them pointed at your own lab AP and test device only.

tools.title: hcxdumptool (PMKID Capture)
tools.description:
Capture packets and PMKID hashes from WLAN devices.
Usage: hcxdumptool -i <iface> -o capture.pcapng --enable_status=1
tools.notes: Actively solicits PMKIDs from APs in range — that is a transmit, so it must be your own AP only. Always use --filterlist_ap/--filtermode to scope to your target BSSID so you don't touch neighbouring networks.

tools.title: hcxtools (PMKID/Hash Conversion)
usage: convert a capture to hashcat 22000 format
list PMKIDs/ESSIDs found in a capture
tools.description:
Convert captured WLAN packets to hashcat/JtR-compatible format.
Usage: hcxpcapngtool -o hashes.txt capture.pcapng
tools.notes: Pure offline conversion — never touches a network. The output feeds hashcat mode 22000 (WPA-PBKDF2/PMKID). Only crack captures from networks you are authorized to test.

tools.title: Bettercap (Network/WiFi/BLE MITM)
usage: start an interactive session on an iface
sudo bettercap -iface eth0 -eval 'set arp.spoof.targets <ip>; arp.spoof on; net.sniff on'
tools.description: Swiss army knife for WiFi, BLE, HID, and Ethernet network recon and MITM attacks.
tools.notes: A live MITM/spoofing framework across WiFi, BLE, and Ethernet — only against hosts and networks you own or are contracted to test. arp.spoof and wifi deauth affect other devices on the segment; scope arp.spoof.targets to a single lab IP.

tools.title: aircrack-ng (WiFi security suite)
usage: capture a handshake on one AP
deauth a client to force a handshake
crack the handshake with a wordlist
tools.description: The core WiFi auditing suite — airmon-ng (monitor mode), airodump-ng (capture), aireplay-ng (deauth/injection), aircrack-ng (WEP/WPA cracking).
tools.notes: airodump/aircrack are passive+offline, but aireplay-ng --deauth transmits and disconnects clients — only ever against your own AP and your own test client. Scope --bssid/-c to a single target so you never disrupt neighbouring networks.

tools.title: Kismet (wireless detector / WIDS)
usage: list detected devices from a log
tools.description: Passive wireless detector, sniffer, and intrusion-detection system — maps APs/clients across WiFi/Bluetooth without transmitting. Ideal for blue-team monitoring and recon.
tools.notes: Kismet is receive-only — it never transmits, so it's the safe way to survey RF. Still, only monitor spectrum you're authorized to observe; passive capture of third-party traffic can be regulated. Runs a local web UI on 127.0.0.1:2501.

tools.title: Reaver (WPS PIN attack)

tools.title: WiGLE (wardriving map & API)
tools.description: Crowd-sourced database mapping hundreds of millions of WiFi/cell networks by BSSID and location — look up an AP you're authorized to assess, or geolocate your own.

tools.title: hashcat example hashes (WPA mode 22000)

tools.title: Aircrack-ng: cracking WPA (tutorial)

tools.title: Cupp

tools.title: crunch (Wordlist Generator)

tools.title: CeWL (Custom Word List)

tools.title: SecLists (Wordlist Collection)

tools.title: DalFox (Finder of XSS)

tools.title: XSS Payload Generator

tools.notes: XSS-LOADER is a menu-driven payload/encoder generator — it builds and encodes payloads for you to test manually. Generating payloads is offline and safe; only fire the results at authorized targets.

tools.title: RVuln

tools.title: kxss (Reflection Finder)

tools.title: PortSwigger — XSS Labs

tools.title: PayloadsAllTheThings — XSS Injection
tools.description: Curated XSS payloads, filter bypasses, and context-specific vectors (attribute, JS, DOM, polyglot).

tools.title: Sigma CLI (Rule Conversion)
usage: convert a whole rules tree to Elastic

tools.title: YARA (Signature Scanning)
usage: compile rules to check for errors
tools.description: Pattern-matching engine for malware families and suspicious artifacts; the signature format most EDR/AV pipelines consume.

tools.title: Suricata (Network IDS)
usage: replay a pcap through the ruleset
tools.description: Signature and protocol-aware IDS/IPS with EVE JSON output that feeds SIEM pipelines.

tools.title: Chainsaw (Event Log Hunting)

extract all detections to a file

tools.title: Hayabusa (EVTX Timeline Analysis)
usage: scan a folder of evtx files
tools.description: Windows event log threat hunting and fast forensics timeline generator driven by Sigma-style rules.
tools.notes: Works on exported logs. Treat generated timelines as sensitive: they contain usernames, hostnames, and process command lines.

tools.title: Zeek (Network Security Monitor)
tools.description: Protocol analyzer that turns traffic into structured connection, DNS, TLS, and file logs.
tools.notes: Live capture needs a mirror/SPAN port and authorization; offline pcap analysis is read-only.

tools.title: Lynis (System Hardening Audit)
usage: sudo lynis audit system --quick | grep -i warning

tools.title: Prowler (Cloud Security Audit)
tools.description: Multi-cloud posture scanner with hundreds of checks mapped to CIS, PCI, HIPAA, and SOC2 controls.

tools.title: auditd (Kernel Audit Rules)

search the audit log for a key

tools.title: CIS Benchmarks

tools.title: Volatility 3 (Memory Forensics)
tools.description: Memory image analysis: processes, network artifacts, injected code, and registry state from a RAM capture.
tools.notes: Acquire memory with a validated tool before rebooting; analyze the copy and keep the hash of the original image.

tools.title: Loki (IOC Scanner)

scan process memory of running apps

collect and parse in one pass

tools.title: Autoruns (Persistence Audit)

tools.description: Wireshark's CLI dissector: filter, follow streams, and extract fields from captures without opening a GUI.
tools.notes: Analyzing your own captures is read-only. Live capture requires an authorized interface and may expose credentials in plaintext protocols.

tools.title: journalctl (Systemd Log Query)
usage: kernel + service messages for a window
tools.description: Query and correlate systemd journal entries across boots and units.
tools.notes: Read-only, but the journal contains IP addresses and account names; treat exports as sensitive.

tools.title: python-evtx (evtx Dump)
tools.description: Pure-Python parser for Windows Event Log (.evtx) files, and the reference implementation used by many toolchains.
tools.notes: Parse copies, never the original evidence file, and hash before/after.

tools.title: lsof (Open Files & Sockets)
usage: who has a deleted-file handle (rootkit smell)
tools.description: Map processes to open files, sockets, and ports — the fastest way to attribute a suspicious listener.
tools.notes: Read-only with sudo; output includes command names and paths that may be sensitive in a shared report.

tools.title: ps / ss (Process & Socket Snapshot)
usage: process tree with full command lines
all TCP sockets with owning process
tools.description: Baseline process trees and socket state with tools guaranteed to exist on the host.
tools.notes: Read-only. Snapshot before and after any containment action so the change is attributable.

tools.title: CAPA (Capability Detection)
tools.description: Maps a binary's code to ATT&CK/MBC capabilities (persistence, C2, credential access) without running it.
tools.notes: Static analysis of a sample you own or were given; keep samples in a password-protected archive and never on a shared filesystem.

tools.title: oletools (OOXML & Macro Analysis)
usage: show only macros with suspicious keywords
tools.description: olevba and friends: extract and deobfuscate VBA macros, detect shellcode, and inspect OLE streams in Office documents.
tools.notes: Parsing does not execute the macro, but Office documents can carry exploit payloads that trigger in a viewer — use a disposable VM.

tools.title: FLOSS (Obfuscated Strings)
tools.description: Mandiant's FLARE Obfuscated String Solver pulls static, stack, and decoded strings that plain `strings` misses.
tools.notes: Emulation of a tiny function region is not full execution, but treat emulated output as untrusted and never run the sample itself outside a sandbox.

tools.title: ClamAV (Signature Scanning)
tools.description: Open-source AV engine and scanner for files, mail, and directories; useful as a first-pass filter.
tools.notes: Signatures lag; a clean scan proves nothing. Never rely on ClamAV alone.

tools.title: Detect It Easy (Binary Inspector)
tools.description: Packer/compiler identification and entropy view for executables — the first thing a reverse engineer checks.
tools.notes: GUI-heavy tool; the CLI build is fine for scripted triage.

tools.title: MISP (Threat Sharing Platform)
usage: docker compose up -d  # from the MISP docker repo
tools.description: Open-source threat intelligence platform for sharing IOCs, events, and taxonomies across teams.
tools.notes: A sharing instance must be access-controlled: feeds contain sensitive indicators and attributions.

tools.title: OpenCTI (CTI Knowledge Base)
tools.description: Structured cyber threat intelligence platform built on STIX 2.1 — actors, campaigns, observables, relationships.
tools.notes: Read intelligence and mapping data; do not publish third-party intelligence without checking its sharing marking (TLP).

tools.title: MITRE ATT&CK Navigator
usage: open the Navigator and load a layer JSON
download layer JSON from the navigator UI
tools.description: Layer editor over ATT&CK technique IDs; used to score coverage and map detections to adversary behavior.
tools.notes: Planning aid only; a colored layer is not evidence that a detection fires.

tools.title: SigmaHQ Rule Repository
usage: git clone https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma && sigma convert -t splunk -p windows sigma/rules/windows
tools.description: The community Sigma rule corpus: vendor-neutral detections that convert to any SIEM backend.
tools.notes: Community rules vary in quality and false-positive rate; test before enabling.

tools.title: YARA Rules Repository
tools.description: Aggregated YARA rules (YARA-Rules/rules plus vendor releases) for family and behavior matching.
tools.notes: Large rule sets are slow; compile them with yarac and scope the scan path.

tools.title: GreyNoise (Internet Noise Context)
usage: look up an IP with the API
tools.description: Contextualizes IPs as internet background noise versus targeted activity — useful for triage de-prioritization.
tools.notes: Context is advisory; an IP marked benign in the mass-scanner sense can still be incidental to your incident.

tools.title: IOC Finder (Indicator Extraction)
tools.description: Extracts and normalizes URLs, domains, IPs, hashes, and emails from free text — turns a report or chat log into indicators.
tools.notes: Defanging is recommended before pasting indicators into tickets or chat.

tools.title: Nuclei (Template Scanning)
tools.description: Template-driven vulnerability scanner with a large community template set; the modern baseline web/network sweep.
tools.notes: Scanning requires authorization for every target in scope; intrusive templates can disrupt fragile services, so rate-limit on production.

tools.title: Trivy (Container & IaC Scanning)
tools.description: Finds vulnerable dependencies, misconfigured IaC, secrets, and OS packages in filesystems, images, and repos.
tools.notes: Local scanning is read-only; image pulls hit the registry and may need auth.

tools.title: OpenVAS / Greenbone (Network Vulnerability Scanner)
usage: list scan configs with the CLI
tools.description: Full network vulnerability management stack with authenticated and unauthenticated scans and a feed of network tests.
tools.notes: A full authenticated scan is intrusive and slow; agree a scan window and exclude fragile OT/medical devices.

tools.title: OWASP Dependency-Check (SCA)
tools.description: Software composition analysis that flags known-vulnerable libraries in a project, with CPE/CPE matching against the NVD.
tools.notes: The initial NVD sync downloads a large dataset; subsequent runs are local.

tools.title: Syft (SBOM Generation)
tools.description: Generates a software bill of materials from images and directories so vulnerabilities can be tracked against known components.
tools.notes: Read-only over local artifacts; SBOMs reveal dependency inventory, so treat them as internal documents.

tools.title: hashcat (GPU hash cracker)
tools.description: World's fastest password recovery tool; cracks 300+ hash types on GPU/CPU.
tools.notes: Cracking is fully offline — it never touches the target. Use -m to match the hash type (hashcat --example-hashes lists them). rockyou.txt lives at /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt on Kali (gunzip it first).

tools.title: John the Ripper (jumbo)
usage: extract a hash from a zip
extract a hash from a PDF
tools.description: Classic CPU cracker with format auto-detect and hundreds of *2john extractors.
tools.notes: Offline only. The *2john helpers (zip2john, ssh2john, pdf2john…) turn a file into a crackable hash — the single most useful thing John does in CTFs.

tools.title: hydra (Network Login Cracker)
usage: stop at first hit, go gentle
tools.description: Fast ONLINE (network) login brute-forcer — throws wordlists at live services: SSH, FTP, RDP, SMB, HTTP forms and 50+ more protocols. The online counterpart to hashcat/John.
tools.notes: Unlike hashcat/John (offline), hydra sends real login attempts to a LIVE service — it's noisy and WILL lock accounts and trip alerts. Authorized targets only. Use -t 4 to slow it down and -f to stop at the first valid credential.

tools.title: CrackStation (online lookup)
tools.description: Free lookup for unsalted MD5/SHA1/SHA256 against a 15B-entry rainbow table. Try before you brute-force.

tools.title: hashes.com (hash identifier + lookup)
tools.description: Identify an unknown hash type and look it up / submit for cracking.

tools.title: CyberChef (the cyber swiss-army knife)
tools.description: In-browser encode/decode, hashing, and data transforms — great for base64, hex, ROT, JWTs.

tools.title: GTFOBins (unix binary abuse)
tools.description: Curated list of how legit unix binaries can be abused for privesc / shell escape — the go-to after a foothold.

tools.title: StegnoCracker
usage: recovered data is written next to it
tools.notes: Fully offline dictionary attack against steghide-embedded files; it shells out to `steghide`, so that must be installed too. rockyou.txt lives at /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt on Kali (gunzip it first). stegcracker is slow and effectively superseded by stegseek — reach for stegseek first.
